We welcome the work of IPES and in particular its landmark nexus and transformative change assessments approved in late 2024 and its more recent assessment on business and biodiversity. For most of the world, the nexus between biodiversity, water, food, health and climate is a framing. For the Pacific, it is daily life. When a reef bleaches, our fisheries and food security suffer together. When a drought hits a small island, freshwater and biodiversity fail together. When the sea rises, we face the prospect of relocating whole communities, carrying their biodiversity, their culture, and their livelihoods with them. The Nexus Assessment's central finding that these crises are interlinked and cannot be solved in silos describes our reality precisely. We ask the convention uptake the convention's uptake of this science do a few things. First, advance a formal biodiversity and climate track. For small island developing states, biodiversity and climate change are one emergency, not two. The best available science is clear. Even meeting the Paris Agreement's one and a half degree Celsius goal is projected to result in the loss of 70 to 90 percent of the world's warm water coral reefs. while a warming of two degrees would result in losses exceeding 99%. At the same time, the world is entering a rapidly strengthening El Nino that forecasts suggest could become the strongest on record, compounding the impacts of human-caused climate change and bringing additional marine heat stress to coral reefs around the globe. A dedicated joined-up science policy process on biodiversity and climate is a longstanding Pacific priority. and this body should support it. Second, make the science ours as well. While we welcome the assessment, we note that developing countries face constraints of limited data, weak monitoring, taxonomic gaps and inadequate financing. We therefore add that under paragraph 2C and 2D, we recognize the gaps and promote technology transfer, scientific cooperation and sustainable financing. We also underscore the importance of integrating indigenous and local knowledge alongside scientific evidence in the assessments and decision making. We support the IPBES midterm review and urge future collaborations to focus on practical implementation guidance and policy tools. Finally, Chair, Kenya recommends that the Executive Secretary supports parties in translating the assessment into national policies and capacity building through their clearinghouse mechanism and technical cooperation mechanism with strengthened investments in biodiversity science and monitoring.
